body.p: These remarks are responsive to the Office action dated June 13, 2023. Prior to entry of this response, claims 1-20 were pending in the application. Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration of the application and allowance of the pending claims.

Unless the next action issued by the Office is a Notice of Allowance, Applicant respectfully requests the Examiner to contact the undersigned representative to schedule a telephonic Examiner interview to discuss whatever issues may still remain after entry of the present response.
Claims 1-20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 on the asserted basis that the claimed invention is directed to an abstract idea of a mental concept of evaluation without significantly more.
Applicant traverses this rejection.

Applicant notes that the first step in evaluating patentable subject matter is determining whether the claim is directed to one of the four patent-eligible subject matter categories: a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter. See USPTO, 2014 Interim Guidance on Patent Subject Matter Eligibility, 79 Fed. Reg. 74618; MPEP §2106(1). In the instant application, claims 1-20 are each directed to a system, which qualifies as a machine.

Therefore, Applicant submits that independent claim 1 and its dependent claims 2-20 are each directed to a patent-eligible subject matter category, and as such pass Step 1 of the patentable subject matter analysis.

The Office asserts at page 2 of the Office action that "[t]he claims fail the first prong of the 2019 Subject Matter Guidance by failing to state with particularity what the system evaluates to enact an error message." Applicant respectfully disagrees. The Office's conclusion of describing the claims as merely being "a mental concept of evaluation" ignores the Federal Circuit's warnings against describing claims at too high a level of abstraction disconnected from the actual claim language. See Enfish, LLC v. Microsoft Corp.,

822 F.3d 1327, 1337 (Fed. Cir. 2016) ("However, describing the claims at such a high level of abstraction and untethered from the language of the claims all but ensures that the exceptions to § 101 swallow the rule."); USPTO, Memorandum - Recent Subject Matter Eligibility Decisions (May 19, 2016). Applicant notes that the claimed features are not directed to a mere "mental concept" as alleged by the Office. Such a reading of the claims is extremely disconnected from the actual claim language.

The 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidelines provide that "[c]laims that do not recite subject matter that falls within [the] enumerated groupings of abstract ideas should not be treated as reciting abstract ideas." 84 Fed. Reg. 50, 53. The Guidelines include groupings of mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity and fundamental economical principles or practices, and mental processes. See 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidelines, 84 Fed. Reg. 50, 52.

Further, the Guidelines state that "[a] claim is not 'directed to' a judicial exception, and thus is patent eligible, if the claim as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application of that exception. A claim that integrates a judicial exception into a practical application will apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the judicial exception." 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidelines, 84 Fed. Reg. 50, 53.

The claims here, even if they recite an abstract idea, which Applicant does not concede, integrate the alleged abstract idea in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception. The claims do not merely generate an error message, which Applicant submits is not an abstract idea, but rather monitor first and second events and subsequently assess compliance of the events with a schedule of events in a particular manner as recited in the claims. The claims thus do not merely gather data and perform a mathematical calculation, but rather monitor multiple events and assess compliance thereof with a schedule in order to generate an error message in response to non-compliance therewith. This is much different than a mere mathematical calculation, and it is performed in unique ways.

"A claim that integrates a judicial exception into a practical application will apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the judicial exception. When the exception is so integrated, then the claim is not directed to a judicial exception." 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidelines, 84 Fed. Reg. 50, 54. The claims clearly integrate any abstract idea allegedly present into a practical application.

Further, "[w]hen making the determination of whether a claim is directed to an abstract idea, examiners should keep in mind that some inventions pertaining to improvements in computer functionality or to improvements in other technologies are not abstract when appropriately claimed, and thus may be eligible at Step 2A." MPEP 2106.04(a)(I). The claims also provide an improvement in vehicle-related functionality, as they improve determinations with regard to determining whether two events are in compliance with a schedule of events and generate an error message in the case of non-compliance. As such, since the claims are also directed to an improvement, they do not recite an abstract idea.

For the above-stated reasons, independent claim 1 and all of the claims depending therefrom are not directed to an abstract idea or any other type of judicial exception, and as such also pass Step 2A of the patentable subject matter analysis. Having passed Step 2A, the analysis would normally end here because claims directed to a statutory patent-eligible subject matter category, and not directed to a judicial exception, are per se eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101. See 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidelines, 84 Fed. Reg. 50, 54.

The second part of Step 2 in evaluating patentable subject matter is to determine whether-when considering the additional elements of the claim, both individually and as an ordered combination-the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception. See USPTO, Memorandum - Formulating a Subject Matter Eligibility Rejection and Evaluating the Applicant's Response to a Subject Matter Eligibility Rejection
(May 4, 2016) at p. 3. As detailed below, even if the claims are construed to be directed to a judicially recognized exception, which Applicant does not concede, the additional claim
elements provide meaningful limitations that render the independent claims patent-eligible subject matter through their application.

The claims in the present application are not directed to an abstract idea, as discussed above, and, even if there is an abstract idea underlying the claimed subject matter, the claims themselves are directed to systems that are founded in concrete, physical instantiations. See DDR Holdings, LLC v. Hotels.com, L.P., 773 F.3d 1245, 1257 (Fed. Cir. 2014) ("[T]hese claims stand apart because they do not merely recite the performance of some business practice known from the pre-Internet world along with the requirement to perform it on the Internet. Instead, the claimed solution is necessarily rooted in computer technology in order to overcome a problem specifically arising in the realm of computer networks" (emphasis added).). Similar to DDR Holdings, LLC vs. Hotels.com, the claims are necessarily rooted in physical technological systems and overcome a problem for handling events that are not in compliance with a given schedule of events. The claims require at least an activity monitor software component configured to generate an error message in situations where the monitored events are not in compliance with the given schedule of events.

As such, Applicant submits that the claims take a particular form and are not merely generic. Therefore, even assuming arguendo that the claims are abstract in nature, which Applicant does not concede as discussed in detail above, their particular forms qualify them as statutory subject matter.
Accordingly, Applicant submits that independent claim 1 and all of the claims depending therefrom are all directed to eligible subject matter.
Consequently, Applicant submits that the 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection of the claims should be withdrawn and such action is respectfully requested.

Applicant submits that several of the dependent claims provide additional features that serve to further establish their subject matter eligibility. For example, claims 5-7 recite a vehicle system, claim 10 recites a speed sensor component, claim 14 recites a vehicle, and claim 17 recites an engine control unit.
body.h1: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. # 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. # 112 (Pre-AIA), First Paragraph
body.p: Claims 1-20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), first paragraph, as failing to comply with the enablement requirement.
Applicant traverses this rejection.

The Office asserts at pages 3-4 of the Office action that "[t]he claims fail to state in such a way that one skilled in the art would be able to construct the invention without undue burden to identify an error in a vehicle powertrain system," and further that "[t]he claims do not identify the sensors used to collect particular data that is measured against a definitive threshold."

Applicant notes that independent claim 1 recites a system having an activity monitor software component that is arranged to "monitor a first event associated with the first software component," "monitor a second event associated with the proxy software component," and "assess compliance of the first and second events with a schedule of events." Applicant submits that the features recited by independent claim 1 do not explicitly recite "sensors" or "a definitive threshold". Applicant further submits that one having ordinary skill in the art would readily recognize the recited terms "first event", "first software component", "second event", "proxy software component", and "assess compliance". As such, Applicant respectfully submits that any specific identification of sensors and definitive thresholds in the claims is simply not necessary for one skilled in the art to construct the invention without undue burden.

Accordingly, Applicant submits that the rejection of independent claim 1 and its dependent claims 2-20 under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), first paragraph, should be withdrawn and such action is respectfully requested.
body.h1: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. # 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. # 112 (Pre-AIA), Second Paragraph
body.p: Claims 1-20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor (or for applications subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, the applicant) regards as the invention.
Applicant traverses this rejection.

The Office asserts at page 4 of the Office action that "[t]he claims do not identify what is measured within the powertrain to determine whether to issue an error message," that "[t]he claims do not identify the thresholds for which a measurement is compared with," and further that "[t]he claims do not identify specific sensors that collect specific data." Firstly, as discussed above, the features recited by independent claim 1 do not explicitly recite "sensors" or "a definitive threshold." Also discussed above, any specific identification of sensors and definitive thresholds in the claims is not necessary.

Applicant notes that the system recited by independent claim 1 is not specifically limited to a powertrain, let alone measurements within a powertrain to determine whether to issue an error message.1 Applicant further notes that the system recited by claim 1 specifies that an error message can be generated responsive to an assessment of "non-compliance [of the first and second events] with the schedule of events." One having ordinary skill in the art would readily understand what is meant by assessing compliance of events with a schedule of events, particularly "wherein assessing compliance includes checking order and/or timing of the first and second events," as recited by independent claim 1.

Accordingly, Applicant submits that the rejection of independent claim 1 and its dependent claims 2-20 under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, should be withdrawn and such action is respectfully requested.
1 Applicant notes that dependent claims 16 and 17 introduce "a powertrain component".

Applicant believes that this application is now in condition for allowance, in view of the above amendments and remarks. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner issue a Notice of Allowability covering the pending claims. If the Examiner has any questions, or if a telephone interview would in any way advance prosecution of the application, please contact the undersigned attorney of record.
